title: Ellipsia Therapeutics — hosting / latency & throughput discovery
summary: Initial discovery focused on Ellipsia's p95 targets for streaming chat (target 250-350ms), batch throughput for inference pipelines, and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted and Dedicated/Private. Customer emphasized regulatory constraints, KMS integration, and predictable tail latencies for live agent assist. Next steps include sharing benchmark plan, security pack, and scheduling a 2-hour deep-dive benchmark run with their infra team.
next_steps: Redwood to share proposed benchmark plan and sample load script by 2026-05-22
Send SOC2 + KMS integration docs to Ellipsia (Maya) by 2026-05-21
Schedule 2hr benchmark window with Priya/Tom for week of 2026-05-25 (Ravi to lead)
Ellipsia to provide representative prompt set and expected token/sequences distribution by 2026-05-22
action_items: Maya Chen: Email pricing tiers & Dedicated capacity options (due 2026-05-21)
Ravi Patel: Draft benchmark runbook + load script (due 2026-05-22)
Priya Nair: Provide sample prompt corpus and token length histogram (due 2026-05-22)
Tom Nguyen: Confirm VPC peering window and firewall rules for benchmark (due 2026-05-24)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. Quick intros?
[00:06] Daniel Ross: Hey Daniel Ross, CTO at Ellipsia.
[00:09] Priya Nair: Priya, Lead ML Eng. We own the inference infra and model serving.
[00:13] Tom Nguyen: Tom, infrastructure, networking and on-prem connectivity.
[00:16] Maya Chen: Great. Ravi from our SEs will walk through the latency and throughput stuff.
[00:19] Ravi Patel: Hi all, hi. Quick agenda: p95 targets you want, streaming token/sec expectations, concurrency and whether you plan hosted or private.
[00:29] Ava Summers: And I just want to make sure the timeline — we need something by end of Q3 for pilot decision.
[00:33] Maya Chen: Noted. Can you share current numbers? Priya?
[00:36] Priya Nair: Sure. For live agent assist we need p95 generation latency around 250 to 350ms for 128 token replies when streaming. For batch inference (reporting) we're more tolerant but throughput needs are like 2000 tokens/sec across a pool during nightly runs.
[00:55] Ravi Patel: OK that's helpful. Are those 250-350ms measured server-side or end-to-end including network?
[00:59] Priya Nair: End-to-end to the agent app. We measured with our proxy and saw a p95 of ~430ms on our current stack which is just raw model hosts. So we need to bring it down.
[01:12] Daniel Ross: Also want tail stability — we can't have spikes above 600ms during business hours.
[01:18] Ravi Patel: Understood. For streaming token/sec — when you say 128 token replies, are you typically streaming tokens or batching and sending full responses?
[01:27] Priya Nair: Streaming for agent assist, yes. For API responses sometimes full. We have mixed workloads.
[01:32] Tom Nguyen: One constraint - we are regulated so data residency in our VPC and KMS integration are must-haves if we go private.
[01:40] Maya Chen: Got it. We'll outline differences between Hosted, Dedicated and Private. Quick question on concurrency — what's your expected concurrent chats during peak?
[01:48] Priya Nair: Expected concurrency is 350-500 concurrent streams during peak. Bursts can go up to 1,200 for a few minutes during incidents.
[01:58] Ravi Patel: That's useful. So we need to size for sustained 500 and allow for burst to 1200 with graceful degradation. Redwood's Dedicated gives predictable capacity and we can reserve headroom; Hosted has autoscaling but tail p95 may vary.
[02:14] Daniel Ross: Cost is a factor — we want predictable unit economics. How do you approach batching vs latency?
[02:21] Ravi Patel: There's tradeoffs. For streaming live messages you minimize batching; that keeps latency low but cost per token is higher. For background jobs you batch heavily to raise tokens/sec and lower cost. We recommend caching prefixes and KV cache for repeated prompts to reduce work.
[02:40] Priya Nair: We've got a lot of repeated system prompts across sessions so prefix caching could help. How does Redwood's KV cache work?
[02:46] Ravi Patel: Briefly: we keep persistent KV cache per conversation on the serving nodes; if a prompt prefix is a hit it avoids recomputing attentions for earlier tokens. It helps a lot for multi-turn. Note — sometimes auto-transcript says K V cash which is wrong, apologies for any transcription artifacts.
[03:05] Maya Chen: We should flag that in the notes. Back to tail latency — do you have SLOs for P99 as well?
[03:11] Daniel Ross: We're focused on p95 right now but P99 alarm would be nice. If p99 goes above 900ms we want alerts.
[03:19] Ravi Patel: Good guardrail. On thread: for hosted we can pin model variants and route requests to a lower-latency quantized variant for default, fallback to higher-accuracy full-precision when quality drop is detected.
[03:34] Priya Nair: Quantized models — we've had trouble with hallucination when quantizing aggressively. Does Redwood Optimize recommend quant profiles by workload?
[03:41] Liam O'Neal: Yeah, we have Optimize suggestions — it looks at sequence length distribution and gives quantization and batching recommendations, plus quality regressions monitored against your eval set.
[03:51] Ava Summers: On compliance — do you have SOC2 and key management integration?
[03:56] Maya Chen: Yes. We are SOC2 Type II. For Private you can bring your KMS/HSM and we integrate via standard KMS APIs. We'll send the security pack.
[04:06] Tom Nguyen: Network-wise, for Private we'll want VPC peering and strict egress rules. For Dedicated, can we get dedicated GPU pools in our cloud account?
[04:15] Ravi Patel: Dedicated means reserved capacity in Redwood-managed clusters; we can also do a hybrid private-control-plane with customer-managed runtime in some setups (more enterprise negotiation). We'll outline options.
[04:26] Daniel Ross: Ok, let's drill into streaming latency — what engineering levers give the most improvement? SDKs? Batching? Kernel selection?
[04:34] Ravi Patel: Biggest wins usually: 1) Use streaming with small chunk sizes to reduce perceived latency; 2) Optimized kernels and compiled paths reduce per-token time; 3) KV caching for multi-turn; 4) Right-sizing instance (GPU type) and sequence length tuning. Also prefix caching and request coalescing for identical prompts.
[04:57] Priya Nair: For benchmarking, we need a reproducible script. Can Redwood run a benchmark with our VPC peering?
[05:03] Ravi Patel: Yes, we can do either: a Redwood-hosted benchmark that simulates your traffic, or a benchmark inside your VPC against a private endpoint. For strict compliance we can run tests within your VPC.
[05:14] Tom Nguyen: That second option is preferred. We'll provide firewall rules and a maintenance window.
[05:19] Maya Chen: Great — we'll prepare a runbook. Any questions about tokens/sec numbers?
[05:25] Priya Nair: For batch jobs we want to saturate a 4-GPU pool and see tokens/sec numbers and p95 across various sequence lengths (64, 256, 1024).
[05:34] Ravi Patel: We'll include those permutations. For streaming we typically report p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec per GPU and system-level concurrent streams supported.
[05:44] Daniel Ross: How do you measure tokens/sec for streaming? Our instrumentation is messy.
[05:49] Ravi Patel: We measure effective token throughput as tokens generated per second aggregated across active streams. For streaming latency we measure from request acceptance to first byte and to full generation completion for p95. We can instrument with their telemetry as well.
[06:05] Priya Nair: Do you support server-side rate limiting and backpressure so our UI doesn't break during a surge?
[06:10] Ravi Patel: Yes — per-route token limits, per-API-key quotas, and graceful fallback policies. We can return a lightweight stub response quickly or route to a cheaper model under heavy load.
[06:20] Ava Summers: And fallback accuracy — are fallbacks transparent? e.g., send a flag when fallback happened so client can degrade gracefully?
[06:27] Ravi Patel: Exactly, we include trace headers and metadata so you can show a degraded indicator in UI or request human escalation.
[06:34] Maya Chen: Let's talk about SLA for Dedicated. Daniel, you mentioned tail stability is important. Our Dedicated offering has contractual p95 targets with credits for miss windows. Would that meet your procurement asks?
[06:45] Daniel Ross: Possibly, yes. We need details on the SLA terms. Also curious about maintenance windows and upgrade path.
[06:51] Maya Chen: We'll send the SLA doc. For maintenance we try to do rolling updates with canary deploys and automatic fallback.
[06:59] Tom Nguyen: One question — does Redwood support mixed-precision kernels on A100s and also Ampere L4s? We plan to test on different GPU classes.
[07:09] Ravi Patel: We support optimized kernels across Ampere and Hopper families; some automatic kernel selection happens during compilation based on model and seq length. We'll include kernel profiles in the benchmark report.
[07:21] Priya Nair: On observability — we need token-level cost breakdown per route, plus per-request traces.
[07:27] Liam O'Neal: Console provides token-level breakdown, per-model dashboards, and tracing hooks you can forward to your tracing system. We can also export raw trace data for your analytics.
[07:36] Priya Nair: Great. A couple of concerns: 1) quantization quality regressions; 2) cold-starts for model shards during spikes; 3) KV cache eviction policies.
[07:47] Ravi Patel: For quantization we recommend running the eval harness; Optimize warns on regressions against your eval prompts. Cold-starts are handled with warm pools and pre-warming strategies; we can reserve warm capacity in Dedicated. KV eviction is LRU by default but configurable.
[08:03] Daniel Ross: For a pilot we probably want Dedicated with private control plane and KMS, but we need to see latency numbers to approve cost.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Totally reasonable. We'll propose a pilot with dedicated capacity sized for 500 sustained streams and burst to 1200 with a small warm pool. The benchmark will prove p95 and tokens/sec.
[08:23] Ava Summers: Timeline check — can you get the security docs this week?
[08:26] Maya Chen: Yes, security pack and SOC2 will be sent tomorrow.
[08:29] Tom Nguyen: On the benchmark runbook — can you include a sample Prometheus/metrics export we can ingest?
[08:34] Ravi Patel: We'll include metrics endpoints and a Grafana dashboard template.
[08:38] Priya Nair: About measuring p95 for streaming: sometimes first byte is low but completion is high; we want both numbers.
[08:45] Ravi Patel: We'll report first-byte p95 and end-to-end generation completion p95 and p99.
[08:52] Maya Chen: Quick off-topic — any competitors you're evaluating?
[08:56] Daniel Ross: We've run small tests with VertexCloud and InferGrid; VertexCloud was lower latency but costlier, InferGrid had jitter. We're benchmarking quality too.
[09:06] Ravi Patel: Perfect — we'll make sure our benchmark uses same inputs for apples-to-apples.
[09:11] Priya Nair: For test data we'll anonymize PHI; we'll scrub anything sensitive.
[09:15] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll sign an NDA if needed for sample data.
[09:19] Daniel Ross: Not necessary if we scrub, but we'll confirm.
[09:22] Ava Summers: Next step recap please?
[09:24] Maya Chen: Sure. Maya to send security docs and pricing. Ravi to share runbook and schedule benchmark. Ellipsia to send prompt set and token histograms. Tom to confirm VPC peering window. Does that match?
[09:35] Everyone: Yes.
[09:37] Ravi Patel: One more technical note — network geometry matters. If your agent UI sits in a region far from the serving region, first byte will add base network latency. We'll include guidance on edge proxies.
[09:50] Tom Nguyen: We'll map regions in the runbook.
[09:53] Maya Chen: Any blockers?
[09:55] Daniel Ross: No blockers, just need the benchmark to be convincing for procurement.
[09:59] Maya Chen: Great — thanks all. We'll follow up with docs and schedule the benchmark.
[10:03] [END]
